what: LivaNova makes implanted medical devices for the nervous system and for heart surgery. Its largest product is a vagus nerve stimulator — a small device implanted in the chest that sends electrical pulses to a nerve in the neck to reduce epileptic seizures and treat depression. It also makes heart-lung machines used in open-heart surgery.
customers: Neurologists and neurosurgeons implanting nerve stimulators, psychiatrists treating resistant depression, and cardiac surgery teams using its heart-lung bypass equipment.
money: Vagus nerve stimulation devices for epilepsy and treatment-resistant depression.
Heart-lung machines, oxygenators and the disposables used in open-heart surgery.
moat: An implanted device creates a patient relationship lasting years: the battery is replaced surgically, and the replacement goes to the same manufacturer because the leads are already in place. Heart-lung machines are capital equipment that then consumes single-use disposables with every operation, which is recurring revenue tied to surgical volumes.
risks: Last year’s results showed a 17.5% net loss margin, and the shares trade at about 26.4 times earnings and 23.3 times EV/EBITDA on the recovery.
Free cash flow of $129.0M against $196.1M of net income, and 39.3 times free cash flow, means the cash generation is thinner than the earnings suggest.
Reimbursement for nerve stimulation in depression has been the central commercial obstacle for years, and the market opens only if payers cover it broadly.
Medtronic and Abbott are far larger competitors in neuromodulation with deeper hospital relationships.
Eleven analysts average a $105.09 target, about 14% above the current price.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $1.0B in 2021 to $1.4B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $1.5B.
Cash of $635.6M against $433.2M of debt is a net cash position.
Implanted devices generate replacement revenue for years because the leads stay in place.
Heart-lung machine disposables are consumed with every operation, which is recurring revenue tied to surgical volume.
Treatment-resistant depression is a large and poorly served population, and a broad reimbursement decision would change the addressable market substantially.
watch: Neuromodulation revenue growth and any change in reimbursement coverage for depression. The epilepsy business is established; depression is the option.
view: LivaNova has one genuinely interesting asset and one solid, unglamorous one. The solid one is cardiopulmonary: heart-lung machines and the disposables consumed in every open-heart operation. That is a steady business tied to surgical volumes, with equipment placed in hospitals that then buys consumables for years. Nothing exciting, nothing fragile.

The interesting asset is vagus nerve stimulation. A small implanted device sends pulses to a nerve in the neck, and it has an established, reimbursed market in drug-resistant epilepsy. The much larger opportunity is treatment-resistant depression — a population that is large, poorly served, and where existing options frequently fail. The clinical case has been building for years. The obstacle has never been the science; it has been whether insurers and Medicare will pay for it at scale.

That makes this stock a reimbursement bet more than a medical device bet, and it is worth being clear about the asymmetry. If broad coverage arrives, the addressable market multiplies and the current revenue base looks like a starting point. If it does not, LivaNova remains a mid-sized device company with a decent epilepsy franchise competing against Medtronic and Abbott, which have far deeper hospital relationships and more resources.

The financial picture supports waiting rather than rushing: $636 million of cash against $433 million of debt means no financing pressure, but free cash flow of $129 million against $196 million of net income and 39 times free cash flow says the cash generation is thinner than the earnings line implies, and 26.4 times earnings already prices in a recovery from last year’s loss. Neuromodulation revenue growth and reimbursement news are the only two things worth watching here.
bull: Broad reimbursement for vagus nerve stimulation in treatment-resistant depression multiplies the addressable market on top of a steady epilepsy and cardiopulmonary base.
bear: Payers keep declining coverage for depression, Medtronic and Abbott press the epilepsy franchise, and a 26 times multiple on recovering earnings unwinds.
